meta.title: Zulu Noun Classes and Sounds
meta.subtitle: 16 noun classes and 23 sounds · both directions, as two cards each
meta.desc: Start here. Two things the Zulu word decks keep naming, learnt before them. 16 NOUN CLASSES: every Zulu noun belongs to a class marked by its prefix — umuntu 'person' is class 1, abantu 'people' class 2, isitolo 'shop' class 7 — and the verb, adjective and pronoun that go with it echo that class, as an adjective echoes gender in French or Hindi. Each note gives the prefix, the kind of noun the class usually holds, the class its plural moves to, its subject concord (the prefix a verb takes with it) and the present of -hamba 'go' with that concord, with an example noun; the classes are numbered as across the Bantu languages, so Zulu has no 12, 13 or 16. 23 SOUNDS: the three clicks — c at the teeth, q at the roof of the mouth, x at the side — each in five kinds (with breath, voiced, nasal, voiced and nasal), and the other sounds English lacks: hl and dl, the two b's, hh, kl, and the difference between ph th kh and p t k. Each is described in English words, never phonetic symbols, with a word that has it. Both directions are asked: see the prefix or the letters and recall what they are, or see the description and recall the prefix or the letters. Sources: the noun class table and concords of Wikipedia's 'Zulu grammar' (which cites Ngcobo 2010, 'Zulu noun classes revisited', South African Journal of African Languages 30(1)) and the sounds of Wikipedia's 'Zulu language', both CC BY-SA 4.0; example words, their meanings and the -hamba forms from English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0).
